title: Mary Magdalene in the garden (John 20:11–18)
hookLine: weeping, she mistakes him for the gardener until he says her name

cards: Grief makes you do strange things. You drive past their house. You keep their voicemail.
You go back to the last place they were. Mary Magdalene goes to the tomb while it's still dark. She had traveled with Jesus and supported him; Luke says he had freed her from seven demons.
She stood at the cross. And now she finds the stone rolled away and the tomb empty. She runs for Peter and the beloved disciple; they come, look, and go home.
But Mary stays outside the tomb, weeping.

teach.h: THEY HAVE TAKEN AWAY MY LORD.
teach.b: She stoops to look in: two angels in white, sitting where his body had been. They ask why she weeps; she says, in the King James Bible: "Because they have taken away my Lord, and I know not where they have laid him."
She turns, and someone is standing there. "Woman, why weepest thou? whom seekest thou?"

She thinks he's the gardener: "Sir, if thou have borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away." She doesn't recognize him. Her eyes are full of tears, and the dead don't stand in gardens.
Then one word: "Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master." That's the moment: not a sermon, not a proof, just her name.

Rabboni means my teacher, a word of closeness. He tells her not to cling to him and sends her to the others; she goes and says: "I have seen the Lord." This is the heart of Christian faith: that Jesus rose from the dead.
And in John the first person to see him, and the first sent to tell it, is a woman who stayed when the others went home.
Early Christian writers called her the apostle to the apostles.
One myth to clear away: the Bible never says she was a prostitute. That idea came from a sermon centuries later that mixed her up with other women in the Gospels.

how: Christians celebrate the resurrection at Easter, the most important feast of the Christian year, often with a vigil or a sunrise service. The Catholic Church keeps Mary Magdalene's feast on July 22, calling her the apostle to the apostles, and Orthodox Christians honor her as equal to the apostles.

games.q: you're Mary. you've found the tomb empty and you're weeping. a man you take for the gardener asks, why are you weeping? whom are you looking for? what do you say?
o: sir, if you've moved him, tell me where, and I'll take him away.
ask him to fetch the disciples.
games.why: she asks the gardener where he has laid him. then he says, Mary, and she turns: Rabboni.

practice: Think of someone who says your name kindly, a grandparent, a friend, a teacher, a partner, someone who's gone, and hear it in their voice; notice what happens in your chest.
In the quiet, let your own name be said kindly, as if by someone who knows you completely and isn't disappointed; if you pray, you can listen for it from God.

wordCard.voice: Rabboni. The word Mary Magdalene cries out the moment she recognizes the risen Jesus, by the sound of her own name, said the way only he said it. These two weeks' words: the keys, transfiguration, Lazarus, hosanna, anamnesis, Gethsemane.

orig.note: Aramaic, kept in John's Greek: my teacher, my master. A word of closeness, the first thing she says when she knows him.

carryVoice: Your line: he said her name. Tomorrow, a road out of Jerusalem. Week ten, complete.
